summary: Updates the description of the IANA registry of vendor subtrees created for ACAP, which is now used by other protocols. It removes the direct normative dependence on ACAP and removes ambiguity.

eli5.summary: A list of company names for private extensions started with one protocol and is used by others. This updates its description so it stands on its own.

what characters are allowed in vendor names
subtitle: A registry for company-specific namespace extensions in Internet protocols

tldr.problem: Several protocols needed a way for vendors to register their own namespace extensions without creating conflicts. The ACAP protocol initially defined a vendor registry, but other protocols have since adopted it.
tldr.mechanism: The registry allows companies to register names starting with 'vendor.' followed by their company or product name, creating private namespaces that can be used across multiple protocols.
tldr.outcome: This RFC clarifies and updates the original ACAP registry specification to make it independent of ACAP and usable by any protocol that needs vendor extensions.

today: RFC 6075 updates RFC 2244 and remains in use today. The ACAP Vendor Subtrees Registry is an Internet Standard that provides vendor namespace extensions for protocols including IMAP ANNOTATE and IMAP METADATA.

sections.title: The Vendor Registry Problem
sections.content:
The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) originally defined a registry for vendor-specific extensions. As described in the RFC, this vendor registry has proven useful and has been adopted by other protocols including IMAP ANNOTATE and IMAP METADATA, making it a general-purpose mechanism.

The registry allows companies and product vendors to reserve portions of a protocol's namespace for private use without needing IANA approval for each extension. This RFC updates the original specification to make the registry independent of ACAP while keeping its essential design.
sections.eli5: When ACAP was invented, it created a system for companies to add their own features without stepping on each other's toes. Now other protocols want to use the same system, so this update makes it stand on its own.

sections.title: Vendor Tokens and Names
sections.content:
A Vendor Token is a string that begins with the literal text vendor. followed by the name of a company or product. For example, vendor.example is a vendor token reserved by a fictional company.

Following the vendor token, additional names can be appended separated by periods, such as vendor.example.product. These extensions need not be registered; any name following the vendor token becomes part of that vendor's namespace.

The complete name is called a Vendor Name, and it is case-sensitive.
sections.eli5: A vendor token is like a company's unique mailbox name. Companies register 'vendor.their-name' and then can make up their own sub-names inside it, like 'vendor.their-name.product-a'.

sections.title: Character Restrictions and Format
sections.content:
To avoid confusion and security issues, the RFC restricts what characters can appear in registered vendor tokens. New registrations are limited to ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, and spaces. This restriction addresses concerns raised after ACAP was published about handling full Unicode strings safely.

The formal syntax, specified in ABNF, is:

vendor-token = "vendor." vendor-tag

Where vendor-tag uses only ALPHA / DIGIT / SP / "-". However, the RFC notes that implementations must still accept non-ASCII Unicode codepoints in vendor tokens for compatibility with future extensions.

Other special characters such as slashes, periods, percent signs, and asterisks are explicitly forbidden in vendor tokens to avoid conflicts with protocol delimiters.
sections.eli5: Only simple characters (letters, numbers, hyphens, spaces) are allowed in the company name part. This keeps things simple and avoids confusion with special symbols used in protocols.

sections.title: The Registration Process
sections.content:
Vendors reserve a vendor subtree by registering with IANA on a first come, first served basis. Once a vendor token such as vendor.example is registered, it is reserved for that vendor everywhere it appears in relevant protocols.

The RFC provides a template for registration requests. A vendor submits to iana@iana.org with the subject line 'Registration of ACAP Vendor Subtree' and specifies the desired vendor token (for example, vendor.companyname) along with contact information.

The RFC emphasizes that vendors should prefer improving interoperable standards over creating private attributes when possible. Once reserved, a vendor name applies consistently across all protocols that use this registry.
sections.eli5: Companies contact IANA and say 'We want vendor.ourname', and IANA keeps a list. First to ask gets it. Once registered, nobody else can use that name in any protocol.

sections.title: Updates from the Original RFC 2244
sections.content:
RFC 6075 makes several clarifications and updates to the original ACAP specification. The key changes include:

First, vendor tokens are now restricted to ASCII characters for registration purposes, addressing security and internationalization concerns.

Second, the RFC clarifies that 'vendor.company.product' means 'vendor.company' followed by '.product', not a structure like 'vendor.company/product' (which is illegal).

Third, the RFC changes the semantics so that 'vendor.company' is itself a valid vendor name that can be registered, not merely a prefix of longer names.

Finally, the RFC adds a concrete example registration for 'vendor.example' to match the example domain names in BCP 32.

At the time of publication, no existing registrations violated the new character restrictions, so backward compatibility was maintained.
sections.eli5: The old rules were a bit vague about what you could do with vendor names. This update makes them clearer, restricts weird characters, and shows a real example of how to register one.
